PHASE 4 · ADVANCED PRIMARY CARE CLINICAL MANAGEMENT

Week 89 — Lesson 113: Skin & Soft-Tissue Infections

FNP-level goal: Distinguish cellulitis from a purulent collection and important noninfectious mimics, select a safe disposition and antimicrobial plan, and immediately escalate when a deep or necrotizing infection is possible.

Learning Objectives

  • Differentiate nonpurulent cellulitis, erysipelas, abscess, purulent drainage, and infected wounds by morphology and physiology.
  • Recognize common cellulitis mimics, including venous stasis dermatitis, edema-related inflammation, contact dermatitis, gout, and deep venous thrombosis when clinically appropriate.
  • Explain why a drainable abscess and nonpurulent cellulitis require different primary management.
  • Apply antimicrobial stewardship: obtain cultures selectively, choose therapy based on syndrome and patient factors, set reassessment expectations, and address recurrence drivers.
  • Identify systemic toxicity, pain out of proportion, crepitus, bullae, necrosis, rapid progression, and failed outpatient therapy as potential deep-infection red flags.

Part 1 — Do Not Diagnose Cellulitis From Color Alone

Redness, warmth, swelling, and pain are findings, not a diagnosis. Cellulitis is a diffuse infection of the dermis and subcutaneous tissue, often presenting as expanding unilateral tenderness, warmth, edema, and poorly demarcated erythema. In darker skin tones, erythema may be subtle or appear violaceous, gray, or hyperpigmented; assess warmth, tenderness, swelling, progression, and systemic symptoms rather than relying on color alone.

Start with a timeline. Ask how quickly symptoms evolved, whether there was trauma, tinea pedis, ulceration, injection, shaving injury, bite, immersion exposure, surgery, chronic edema, diabetes, immunocompromise, prior MRSA, or recent antibiotics. Compare both limbs. A bilateral, chronic, itchy, scaling, or minimally tender lower-extremity process should slow the clinician down before labeling it bilateral cellulitis.

Part 2 — Nonpurulent Cellulitis and Erysipelas

Nonpurulent cellulitis has no drainable collection or purulent drainage. Erysipelas is often described as a more superficial infection with a more sharply demarcated border, although terminology varies. The management question is not which label sounds more precise; it is whether the syndrome is diffuse and nonpurulent or whether pus is present and needs source control.

For uncomplicated nonpurulent cellulitis in a stable patient, antimicrobial selection should target the likely syndrome and be tailored to allergies, renal function, pregnancy status when relevant, local practice, severity, and follow-up reliability. Routine swab, blood, aspirate, or biopsy cultures are not useful for every typical outpatient cellulitis presentation. Cultures become more relevant with severe systemic illness, treatment failure, unusual exposures, animal bites, immersion injury, immunocompromise, or an atypical presentation.

Part 3 — Abscess: Source Control Comes First

An abscess is a localized collection of pus. It is commonly painful, tender, fluctuant, and may have a pustular center or spontaneous drainage. A patient may call it a boil or spider bite, but the FNP must determine whether a drainable collection is present. Point-of-care ultrasound can be useful when the examination cannot distinguish cellulitis from an occult fluid collection, if available and within training and local protocols.

The central principle is source control: a drainable abscess generally needs incision and drainage rather than antibiotics alone. Antibiotics may be adjunctive in selected situations, such as systemic illness, impaired host defenses, severe disease, failure of initial management, extensive surrounding infection, or other patient-specific risk. The procedure, culture decision, analgesia, aftercare, and follow-up must be planned deliberately. Calling every purulent lesion cellulitis can delay the treatment that actually matters.

Part 4 — Purulent Versus Nonpurulent Changes the Clinical Question

For diffuse nonpurulent cellulitis, the primary treatment question is antimicrobial coverage for the likely pathogens and management of predisposing factors. For a purulent collection, the primary question is whether it needs drainage and whether adjunct antibiotics or culture are indicated. MRSA risk should be considered in compatible purulent infections, but it should not become a reflex reason to use broad or multiple antibiotics for every red leg.

Antimicrobial stewardship means choosing the narrowest reasonable strategy for the syndrome, documenting why broader coverage is needed when it is, reviewing allergy history carefully, and giving clear return precautions. It also means stopping the diagnostic search too late is not safe: worsening, absence of expected improvement, or a changing exam requires reassessment of diagnosis, source control, adherence, pathogen, vascular disease, and deeper infection.

Part 5 — Mimics: A Red Leg Is Not Always an Infected Leg

Common mimics include venous stasis dermatitis, chronic venous insufficiency, lymphedema-related inflammation, contact dermatitis, inflammatory arthritis or gout, superficial thrombophlebitis, hematoma, and deep venous thrombosis when the history and risk factors support it. Some patients have both venous disease and true infection. The FNP should ask whether the process is acute or chronic, unilateral or bilateral, painful or pruritic, febrile or afebrile, and whether edema, varicosities, scale, dermatitis, or a portal of entry is present.

A correct diagnosis avoids unnecessary antibiotics, but a competing diagnosis must never be used to dismiss worsening pain, systemic symptoms, or objective progression. Diagnostic humility and scheduled reassessment are safety tools.

Part 6 — Find and Treat the Portal of Entry

Recurrent lower-extremity cellulitis often has modifiable contributors: chronic edema, skin breakdown, fissured toe webs, tinea pedis, venous disease, wounds, obesity, or poorly fitting footwear. Examine the feet and interdigital spaces when appropriate. Elevation, edema management, skin care, treatment of an underlying dermatosis or fungal disease, and wound prevention may reduce recurrence more effectively than repeatedly extending antibiotics.

For recurrent abscesses, ask about previous cultures, household or close-contact clusters, injection exposures, hidradenitis suppurativa, foreign material, and location-specific disease. Decolonization approaches and specialist plans are individualized; do not offer a one-size-fits-all promise of permanent eradication.

Part 7 — Wounds, Diabetes, and Host Factors

Skin infection in a patient with diabetes, peripheral artery disease, neuropathy, lymphedema, chronic ulceration, renal disease, cancer therapy, or immunosuppression deserves a lower threshold for careful examination and escalation. These factors do not automatically require hospitalization or the broadest antibiotics, but they change the consequences of a missed deep infection and the reliability of clinical findings.

For a foot wound, examine perfusion, sensation, depth, drainage, surrounding tissue, foreign-body risk, and ability to offload or follow up. Do not treat a potentially complex diabetic foot infection as ordinary uncomplicated cellulitis. Infection, ischemia, neuropathy, and osteomyelitis risk require their own structured assessment.

Part 8 — Necrotizing Soft-Tissue Infection: The Safety Diagnosis

Necrotizing soft-tissue infection is uncommon but time-critical. Early skin findings may resemble uncomplicated cellulitis, so the FNP must recognize the mismatch between the patient and the skin. Red flags include severe pain out of proportion to the visible findings, rapidly progressive swelling or erythema, systemic toxicity, hypotension, altered mental status, wooden-hard induration, edema extending beyond the erythema, bullae, ecchymoses, skin anesthesia, necrosis, or crepitus.

Suspected necrotizing infection requires emergency escalation and prompt surgical consultation. Imaging may sometimes help answer a question in a stable patient, but it must not delay definitive evaluation when clinical suspicion is high. Antibiotics are important, but they do not substitute for operative assessment and source control when a necrotizing process is possible.

Part 9 — Follow-Up Is Part of the Prescription

Before outpatient treatment, confirm that the patient is hemodynamically stable, can take the plan as prescribed, understands wound care or drainage instructions, has access to follow-up, and knows exactly when to return. Marking an advancing border can help a patient and clinician recognize true progression, but the overall clinical picture matters more than a line on the skin.

Give explicit return precautions: spreading redness, escalating pain, new fever, weakness, confusion, vomiting, rapid drainage change, new bullae, dark discoloration, numbness, inability to use the limb, or no expected improvement. At reassessment, do not simply prescribe a second antibiotic; revisit whether the original diagnosis and source-control plan were correct.

Part 10 — FNP Case: The Purulent Lesion

A 29-year-old has a very tender axillary nodule with a pustular center and palpable fluctuance. The key question is not only which antibiotic to select. The clinician evaluates for a drainable abscess, systemic illness, host risk, surrounding spread, and HS history. If a collection is present, source control is central; antibiotics and culture decisions are then individualized to severity and risk.

Part 11 — FNP Case: The Red Leg That Is Not Cellulitis

A 71-year-old has months of bilateral lower-leg edema, hyperpigmentation, scale, and itch, without fever or focal tenderness. Treating this as bilateral cellulitis with repeated antibiotics misses likely venous and inflammatory contributors. The FNP documents the chronic pattern, evaluates competing diagnoses and vascular risk appropriately, addresses skin and edema care, and establishes follow-up with return precautions if acute infection develops.

Part 12 — FNP Case: Do Not Delay Surgical Evaluation

A patient with diabetes develops rapidly worsening thigh pain after a minor abrasion. The pain is severe, vital signs are abnormal, and the swelling extends beyond the visible redness. This is not a routine outpatient cellulitis escalation. The priority is emergency transfer and surgical-capable evaluation for a possible deep or necrotizing infection.

FNP High-Yield Framework

  1. Classify: diffuse nonpurulent process, purulent/drainable collection, wound-associated infection, or mimic.
  2. Assess severity: vital signs, systemic toxicity, rapid progression, pain, host factors, location, function, and follow-up reliability.
  3. Source control: a drainable abscess is not treated as cellulitis alone.
  4. Prescribe deliberately: choose syndrome-directed antimicrobial therapy when indicated; culture selectively; avoid unnecessary breadth and duration.
  5. Prevent recurrence: find portals of entry, manage edema and skin disease, and address wound or HS patterns.
  6. Escalate immediately: suspected necrotizing infection, sepsis, severe pain, bullae/necrosis/crepitus, rapidly progressive disease, or unstable patients need emergency care.

Take-Home Summary

Safe SSTI care begins with diagnosis, not an antibiotic reflex. Nonpurulent cellulitis, purulent abscesses, chronic inflammatory mimics, and deep necrotizing infections have different pathways. The FNP protects patients by identifying source control needs, using antibiotics thoughtfully, treating recurrence drivers, scheduling reassessment, and moving quickly when the patient’s pain, toxicity, or progression suggests a deeper process.

Educational note: This lesson supports clinical reasoning and does not replace individualized diagnosis, current prescribing information, local resistance patterns, procedure training, local protocols, specialist guidance, or emergency evaluation when red flags are present.
